intake: agnostic — seminary-trained, left without settling it; I think theism is a live question that neither the proofs nor the disproofs I've seen close.

walk.note: This is biography, not argument, but it is how I got there, so yes.
Looking for God in the world rather than the text is exactly what I did; note that Aquinas held Religion and Classical theism at once, they are not successive stops.
Classical theism does not deny that God is a subject who wills and chooses; Aquinas's God creates freely. The dilemma is aimed at a position nobody at my seminary held.
No serious theology predicts that surgical outcomes track petitionary prayer; STEP refutes a vending machine, not God.
'Not denied' and 'does not seem to reduce' get you to 'dualism is possible', not to dualism.
Dependence is not identity, but the interaction problem is enough to move me off dualism.

'Physics gives structure not what has it' is the Russellian point, and it is compatible with several views; it does not deliver 'reality is at bottom mind', and 'if physicalism is true the floor is contestable' reads backwards.
Even Lichtenberg's 'it thinks' grants that thinking is going on; but 'the universe is not a brain' smuggles physicalism back into a position we supposedly left.
I would make the same choice, though I would call it decency rather than mercy.
Acting kindly ahead of proof does keep your ignorance in view; the entropy paragraph and the 'author's or Claude's' line mean nothing to me and should go.
The author says hope is a choice and that acknowledged limits equally allow a secular hope; I choose equanimity, and I do not have the second naïveté this position names.
The move says the maker must be a resolved mind and then concedes that being a maker does not make a maker resolved; it undercuts itself in two sentences.
'More of a bargain than an argument' is the whole move; what bargain, between whom, for what?
'To think is to ignore' is a fact about finite minds generalized to every possible mind without argument, and the move itself admits Aquinas's non-discursive knowing has not been shown incoherent.
Granting no maker, the good in beings is where I would put it too; Euthyphro already pointed this way.
The move says the need to be remembered is a motive, not evidence; a motive for a question is not a position, and the position's own text admits it is not dualism.
There is no move here to take or refuse; 'both the ceiling and the floor' is a phrase, not a claim.

first_exit.why: The hiddenness dilemma ends with 'a God who chooses is a subject: the personal God that classical theism denies', and that is simply false; Aquinas's God has intellect and will and creates freely. I am agnostic, but not because of an argument against a God no classical theist proposed.

comment: Your first turn argues against a God who answers prayer on demand and whom classical theism supposedly denies is personal, and anyone who has read Aquinas will get off at move 3 and never trust the rest; if you want the atheism moves to carry, argue against the God Aquinas actually described. The second turn's two decisive moves, 15 and 16, are respectively empty and self-confessedly unproven, so the whole second spiral rests on a bargain you never state and a premise you admit you have not established. Also, rename Dualism₂: you say yourself it is not dualism.
